workIntro.lead: A bunch of projects from over the years. Some ended up on thousands of devices, some were failures, but all of them taught me something.

career.blurb: Started my development career at Letink, a digital 3D agency, as an intern. After that i got hired as a VR developer to develop immersive experiences and support during conventions.
career.detail: My developer career began at Letink Design, building VR and AR applications for the construction sector, tourism and government — publishing them online and supporting clients on location at trade fairs and events. On the side I made explainer animations, built interactive installations and assembled the office PCs myself.

career.blurb: DTT is a development studio where I worked across gaming and XR projects and grew from intern to team lead
career.detail: At DTT I started as an intern and grew into helping lead a team of developers across VR, Android, iOS and web projects. My responsibilities included selecting and mentoring new developers, improving the team's ways of working, and building features like deep linking, iOS plugins, XR, multiplayer, in-app purchases and optimisation.

career.blurb: For Zwijsen i designed, built and shipped AR seek-and-find and audiobook apps for children's books.
career.detail: As a freelancer for publisher Zwijsen I built AR seek-and-find and audiobook apps for children's books — designed, developed and published from A to Z on Zwijsen's store pages. The apps were opened through QR codes in the books and gathered tens of thousands of downloads with exclusively positive reviews.

career.blurb: At Popcore i made casual mobile games for large audiences. These apps are on millions of devices and have to stay fun AND stable to keep users engaged for a long time.
career.detail: Looking for a new challenge I joined Popcore to build hyper-casual games for a huge Android and iOS audience. I ran live-ops on titles like Parking Jam, Pull the Pin and Wrecking Ball, and implemented new game modes, multiplayer features and tools for editors and level designers — everything on an ECS framework for speed and flexibility. Popcore is where I grew fastest as a developer: a place that challenges you to keep sharpening yourself to make games that actually perform in the crowded mobile market.

career.blurb: Wonderment specializes in Location-based XR. Anchoring digital experiences to real places to tell new and interesting stories, that's what i made happen working here.
career.detail: I joined Wonderment to follow my enthusiasm for AR, building location-based experiences: visualisations, games and web applications, plus R&D into image recognition with machine learning in Unity and Lens Studio. My biggest focus was VPS and Cesium — technology that pins AR to the outside world with centimetre accuracy — enriching environments with geodata like GIS, 3D map tiles and geoJSON. I'm especially proud of leading the development of a multiplayer race game and a photo installation for Niantic: a constant balance between testing risky techniques and hitting deadlines, a challenge I took on with pleasure.

career.blurb: Medical XR and AI prototyping. Worked at the immersive lab on pushing new spatial tech toward something dependable enough to actually be useful.
career.detail: At Philips' immersive lab I visualised medical equipment and built VR experiences that are both educational and informative — used to familiarise people with new medical developments and to present them at trade fairs.

career.blurb: For Alliander i worked on integrating XR into their operations. In a small dedicated team we made a prototype for placing energy transformers in the real world.
career.detail: For Alliander I built HoloLens software that lets field crews enrich their surroundings with information from the grid database, making the construction of medium-voltage stations more efficient. I was responsible for the development, optimisation and UX of these apps, alongside innovation projects like visualising entire neighbourhoods through 3D scanning. Alliander taught me that complex applications demand knowledge from many angles — finding the KPIs that matter and deciding who to involve was an interesting challenge in itself.

career.blurb: Worked at the Philips immersive lab on pushing new spatial tech toward something dependable enough to actually be useful.
career.detail: Back at the immersive lab: pushing new spatial tech toward something dependable enough to actually be useful, including research into how Apple Vision Pro could be applied within Philips. The freedom to test new techniques and judge whether they hold real value made this the most instructive part of my recent years.

career.blurb: The Marechaussee is the Dutch military police. I worked on a project to connect VR players in a complex simulation framework that has been in development for years.
career.detail: The Marechaussee is the Dutch military police. I work on connecting VR players inside a complex training system that has been in development for years — multiplayer networking where failure isn't an option.

about.title: making computers do unusual things since 2016
about.lead: I’m a creative technologist from Utrecht. For almost a decade I’ve been chasing the same little moment: when a piece of technology stops feeling like technology and starts feeling like a small magic trick.
body: Most of my work is somewhere between the screen and the real world. I’ve built things that put virtual objects in public spaces, turned books into interactive worlds, connected strangers through AR. I like being close to the machine, diving into the pixels, the code, the hardware, the people using it and what happens when it all has to connect.

A lot of what i know came from breaking things, sometimes on purpose. I like finding technology when documentation is still incomplete and everyone is still figuring out what it can do. Like ARKit before it had a dev-friendly abstraction layer or Multiplayer AR before the tools were ready. The unfinished parts are usually where the interesting questions are.

I have a theory i keep coming back to: the demo lies to you. A prototype on my desk can look like the future, but the real world always gets the final word. Networks disappear, hardware behaves strangely and someone will always use my carefully designed interface in a way i never imagined.

Right now I’m connecting VR players for the department of defense, with all the security constraints you can imagine come with that, i'm experimenting with an art installation using projection mapping and keeping up to date with the latest AI frameworks. If you like thinking about what technology can do, we’ll probably have something to talk about!
